problem: VLN research is benchmark-driven and simulation-bound, with diverse methods lacking a clear taxonomy and lacking systematic real-world validation, so the practical effectiveness and sim-to-real gap of existing approaches is unclear.
motivation: SoTA VLN methods reach very high SR in idealized simulation, but real robots face motion blur, collisions, odometry drift and ambiguous instructions. A survey organized by action and model paradigms, plus a controlled physical-robot comparison, reveals which design choices matter for deployment.
key_idea: Organize VLN methods along two orthogonal axes (hierarchical vs monolithic action paradigm; discriminative vs generative model paradigm) and validate representative systems (CLASH vs JanusVLN) on a wheeled robot across 10 real scenes.
insight: In the real-world test, the hierarchical panoramic + LiDAR/SLAM system reached SR 51% and CR 7%, while the monolithic RGB-only system had SR 22% and CR 51%, despite 61% SR in simulation. The gap is confounded by sensing (panorama vs monocular), memory (topological graph) and geometric sensing (LiDAR), so it is not a pure architecture effect. Strict semantic stopping (SSR) lowers hierarchical SR from 51% to 37%, and both systems fail on stopping for intention/backtracking instructions.
method: Taxonomy: two orthogonal axes, action paradigm (hierarchical waypoint-based vs monolithic action-based) and model paradigm (discriminative vs generative), giving four quadrants with a timeline and statistics.
Literature review: covers datasets, simulators, metrics and problem formulation (POMDP; discrete graph vs continuous), plus strengths and limitations of each paradigm.

Real-robot platform: differential-drive wheeled robot with Jetson Orin Nano, Mid-360 LiDAR, and a camera on a 1.5 m tripod (Insta360 X4 panoramic or RealSense D435i RGB-D); inference offloaded to an L40 server over Wi-Fi.
Baselines: hierarchical CLASH (panoramic, SLAM point-goal waypoints, Qwen2.5-VL-72B via API) vs monolithic JanusVLN (single-view RGB, step-wise discrete actions with PID control).
Protocol: 10 scenes x 10 tasks, 100 episodes per method, same starts and instructions; 70% R2R-style, 20% intent-ambiguous, 10% multi-stage backtracking; unseen scenes.
New metrics: Strict Success Rate (SSR, requires semantic correctness of the stop location) and Collision Rate (CR, episode terminates on collision).

setting.backbone: CLASH (hierarchical; small model + Qwen2.5-VL-72B via API) and JanusVLN (Qwen2.5-VL-7B + VGGT, monolithic); both used off-the-shelf
setting.training_data: none (existing pretrained models evaluated without new training)
setting.observation: Hierarchical: 360° panoramic RGB (Insta360 X4) + LiDAR/SLAM; monolithic: single-view RGB (RealSense D435i)
setting.action_space: Hierarchical: SLAM-based point-goal waypoints; monolithic: step-wise discrete actions (turn 15°, forward 25 cm, stop) with a PID controller
setting.privileged: none (LiDAR-SLAM localization and mapping used by the hierarchical system)

numbers.eval_set_note: 100 episodes per method across 10 real scenes, each run once
numbers.extra: panoramic camera + LiDAR/SLAM waypoints; no panoramic depth; same start/instructions as monolithic
numbers.evidence: Sec. Average Performance Comparison: 'hierarchical configuration attains ... SR of 51%, an SSR of 37%, and an OSR of 67%'; 'CR of 7%'

numbers.eval_set_note: 100 episodes per method across 10 real scenes, each run once
numbers.extra: single-view RGB from RealSense D435i; no LiDAR
numbers.evidence: 'monolithic configuration achieves an SR of 22%, an SSR of 17%, and an OSR of 27%'; 'high CR of 51%'

numbers_note: Per-scene, intention/backtracking (hier. SR 35% vs 25% on intention, 0% vs 20% on backtracking), and timing results are given mainly in figures. The survey does not report new benchmark simulation results itself.
results: In 200 real-world episodes across 10 scenes, hierarchical CLASH gets SR 51%/SSR 37%/OSR 67%/CR 7% versus monolithic JanusVLN SR 22%/SSR 17%/OSR 27%/CR 51% (JanusVLN reaches 61% SR in simulation). Hierarchical needs fewer inference steps and less total time, but is worse on backtracking.
limitations: Real-world comparison confounds architecture with sensing (panoramic vs monocular), LiDAR/SLAM and control stack, and covers only two systems with 100 episodes each.
Single run per episode (seed 42), and the SSR semantic-correctness annotation is manual.
Inference is offloaded to a remote server, so latency depends on the network; low-level obstacles below the LiDAR plane still cause collisions.
